paper_title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

Introduction As Carl Sagan observed, Science is way of thinking much more than it is body of knowledge. Scientific discovery involves more than producing new hypotheses or accumulating findings. It unfolds through an iterative loop: scientific search generates and tests ideas, scientific understanding develops through the interpretation of the resulting findings, and this understanding guides subsequent search [1]. Researchers move within and between hypothesis and experiment spaces around scientific question, proposing explanations, designing tests, and interpreting experimental, computational, or observational feedback [2]. Interpreting this feedback develops working understanding of the problem: which judgments are supported, which conflicts remain unresolved, under which conditions findings apply, and which regularities may transfer across cases. As understanding changes, researchers revise hypotheses, reformulate questions, redesign experiments, and reassess which direction merits further effort. Classical problem-solving research describes how representations, operators, and heuristics organize this search and guide subsequent action [3, 4]. The central design question is how to retain the understanding developed during search and use it to select and adapt representations, operators, and heuristics, so that search experience informs subsequent research decisions. Recent AI systems have extended one-shot idea generation into iterative scientific workflows. The AI Scientist connects ideation with experiments, analysis, and paper writing [5]; Co-Scientist organizes hypothesis generation, critique, and improvement [6]; and Robin combines multi-agent reasoning with experimental feedback [7]. Iteration alone, however, does not ensure that findings from different branches are retained with their evidence and applicability conditions, or that these findings affect later method selection. When iteration depends mainly on feedback from the current round, earlier failures, unresolved conflicts, and shared dependencies can be overlooked, leading to repeated errors or further search along unproductive paths. Search can also become overly responsive to recent outcomes, delaying recognition of key uncertainties or change in targets, representations, or reasoning methods. scientific agent therefore needs to preserve understanding across the search and use it to regulate what to investigate next and how to investigate it. This need motivates drawing on metacognition, concept rooted in the study of human cognition. Often described as thinking about thinking, metacognition involves monitoring, and regulation of ones own cognitive processes [8]. Nelson and Narens distinguish an object level that performs task from meta level that maintains dynamic model of the object-level cognition and regulates its process through monitoring and control [9]. Prior work examines how artificial systems can monitor and adjust their own problem-solving processes [10], complementary research on strategy selection motivates matching reasoning methods to the task and current state [11]. Viewed through the lens of metacognition, object-level search develops scientific understanding, while the meta level selectively represents this understanding and assesses its implications for further search, guiding decisions about which premises to examine, representations to revise, methods to apply, or branches to stop. We adopt this functional distinction as architectural inspiration for explicit search regulation. We introduce Sage-Taiyi, metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. SageTaiyi achieves leading performance on Taiyi-Bench, AgentIdeaBench, and IG-Arena. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, it ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. Method Sage-Taiyi is metacognition-inspired architecture for scientific discovery in which the search for ideas and the understanding of the scientific problem develop together. Section 2.1 defines the object and meta levels and how they interact. At the object level, scientific search constructs and transforms ideas across target branches (Section 2.2). At the meta level, Cognitive State selectively represents object-level scientific understanding and records monitoring assessments, while Cognitive Repertoire retains reusable methods (Section 2.3). Monitoring and control connect the two levels (Section 2.4), and research harness links ideas to planning, tool use, and external validation (Section 2.5). 2 2.1. System Overview Sage-Taiyi organizes scientific discovery into two levels, drawing on accounts of discovery as problem solving [3, 12] and of metacognition as monitoring and control of thinking [13, 14]. Figure 2 Sage-Taiyis two-level scientific search and monitoringcontrol loop. The architecture comprises object-level scientific search and meta-level metacognitive regulation. The object level includes Target Tree that organizes targets, subtargets, local strategies, and subideas; an Idea Graph that records ideas and their lineage; and an Evidence State that retains experimental results, literature knowledge, and expert input. The meta level includes Cognitive State that maintains selective representation of object-level scientific understanding alongside monitoring-derived assessments, and Cognitive Repertoire that provides reusable methodological heuristics and Cognitive Operators. Monitoring and control coordinate the two levels: the Target Tree guides idea exploration, the Idea Graph reveals gaps encountered during exploration, and the Evidence State grounds evaluation. Monitoring uses these inputs to update the Cognitive State, assessing evidential support, uncertainty, shared dependencies, and their implications for search. Control uses the Cognitive State to select applicable heuristics and operators and guide subsequent scientific actions, enabling scientific understanding and the search for novel ideas to evolve together. The object level addresses the scientific problem itself, carrying out scientific search for research question 𝑞. As in problem-space accounts of discovery, this search moves between knowledge states through local transformations [3, 1]. Its state is 𝑋𝑡 = (𝑇𝑡, 𝐺𝑡, 𝐸𝑡): the Target Tree 𝑇𝑡 organizes targets and subtargets, the Idea Graph 𝐺𝑡 records ideas and their lineage, and the Evidence State 𝐸𝑡 retains experimental and computational results, literature knowledge, and expert input with their sources. Decomposing targets, generating, transforming, and evaluating ideas, and judging what the evidence supports are object-level operations, as is the integration of these judgments into scientific understanding. The meta level assesses how scientific search is proceeding and decides how it should be adjusted [8]. It maintains two resources. The task-specific Cognitive State 𝐶𝑡 records what the search has established about the problem and what this implies for further search (Section 2.3.1). The reusable Cognitive Repertoire contains methodological heuristics, which organize research paths, and Cognitive Operators, which perform local reasoning transformations between knowledge states (Sections 2.3.22.3.3). Selecting methods to regulate scientific search is meta-level decision; applying them to develop targets or ideas is object-level search. Monitoring and control connect the two levels [9]. Object-Level Scientific Search 2.2.1. Target Tree: Decomposing the Research Question The Target Tree decomposes the research question into more specific targets and subtargets. Its root is 𝑞, and each node is target or subtarget that records its scientific requirements and completion criteria. Under methodological heuristic selected by control, target is decomposed into subtargets; each subtarget is paired with local strategies for addressing it, and each strategy yields subideas, partial solutions that can later be assembled into complete ideas. This structure follows problemspace accounts in which problem is reduced to subproblems that are solved by applying operators [3, 12]. The tree is not fixed at the outset: as ideas develop, subtargets are added or revised while the root question and its constraints are retained (Section 2.2.2). 2.2.2. Idea Graph: Developing Ideas across Branches Ideas are the units that Sage-Taiyi evaluates, transforms, and outputs. An idea is complete proposal specifying mechanism or design, supporting references, constraints, testable consequences, and the uncertainties to be examined. The Idea Graph records ideas as nodes and their transformations as edges. Ideas enter the graph by assembling subideas from the Target Tree or by direct generation from the research question, with or without selected heuristic. Because the graph spans target branches, ideas developed for different targets can be compared and recombined. Five transformations, informed by population-based search and conceptual combination [15, 16, 17, 18], produce new ideas. Merge consolidates ideas that take similar approaches; Fuse combines complementary mechanisms from different ideas after checking that their assumptions and interfaces are compatible; Diverge keeps an idea and opens substantively different branch from it; Repair fixes defective dependency or missing interface; and Evolve improves an idea while 4 retaining its core mechanism. Over successive iterations, these transformations can refine ideas and combine strengths developed for different targets. As ideas develop, they can expose requirements that no current target covers, motivating new subtargets in the Target Tree. To keep this development traceable, each new idea is linked to its parents and to the evaluation that motivated it. 2.2.3. Evidence State: Grounding Scientific Understanding The Evidence State grounds scientific search in external information. It records experimental and computational results, literature knowledge, and expert input, linking each to its source, relevant ideas, and conditions. Using this evidence, the object level forms scientific judgments, for example which mechanisms are supported, under which conditions findings hold, and which explanations conflict. Each judgment retains its evidential grounds, allowing new evidence to inform revisions to relevant judgments and their dependencies while preserving unaffected alternatives. Judgments formed in one branch can also inform reasoning in others. Integrated across branches, these evidencegrounded judgments and their relations form the systems current scientific understanding of the problem [19, 20]. 2.3. Meta-Level Representations and Resources While the object level develops targets and ideas, the meta level keeps track of how this search is proceeding and adjusts its course. The meta level regulates scientific search with two resources. The Cognitive State represents the current search and is revised by monitoring as new findings or assessments warrant an update. The Cognitive Repertoire retains reusable method knowledge: methodological heuristics, which organize research paths, and Cognitive Operators, which transform knowledge states. 2.3.1. Cognitive State: Representing the Current Search Following Nelson and Narens account of the meta level as maintaining dynamic model of objectlevel cognition [9], the Cognitive State models the current search. It contains two kinds of content. The first is selective, source-linked representation of object-level scientific understanding, retaining key findings, competing explanations, necessary assumptions, applicability conditions, and unresolved questions. The second consists of monitoring-derived assessments of the evidential status of key judgments, unresolved conflicts and uncertainties, and dependencies shared across ideas. The former selectively represents what the system currently understands about the scientific problem; the latter assesses how this understanding should guide further search. For example, when several ideas propose different mechanisms but depend on the same untested premise, monitoring records that they share potential failure condition and that their agreement does not provide independent support. The two kinds of content describe functions of the state rather than separate storage modules. Monitoring revises both as new evidence and evaluations of ideas emerge (Section 2.4.1), preserving sources and keeping working hypotheses distinct from external evidence. Control uses the revised state to select methods from the repertoire and determine subsequent research actions; their application updates targets and ideas (Section 2.4.2). 2.3.2. Methodological Heuristics: Organizing Research Paths Methodological heuristics organize complete research workflows. Since the space of possible research paths is too large to search exhaustively, scientists in different disciplines develop characteristic research paradigms that lead them to workable solutions more efficiently [3, 4, 21, 22]. Drawing 5 on these accounts, Sage-Taiyi organizes related reasoning principles into ten methodological heuristics for reusable research workflows (Figure 3 and Table 1). Each heuristic specifies when it applies, how it decomposes target into subtargets and local strategies, coordinates cognitive operators, and evaluates the resulting ideas. Figure 3 Methodological heuristics. The ten heuristics organize recurring strategies for scientific research grounded in evidence, models, analogies, representations, goals, and practical constraints. These general heuristics are further instantiated with discovery methods summarized from the literature of specific research domains (Section 2.3.4). Control selects heuristics according to the research question and the current Cognitive State [11], and the selected heuristics guide the construction of the Target Tree (Section 2.2.1). Cognitive Operators: Transforming Knowledge States Drawing on problem-space accounts of human problem solving [3], Sage-Taiyi defines Cognitive Operators as local reasoning transformations reusable across methodological workflows. Backward 6 reasoning infers conditions or subgoals from an outcome; inverse design also constructs and validates design. Mechanism integration aligns existing mechanisms interfaces and assumptions to form candidate; compositional synthesis also decomposes the target and evaluates the system. Operators act on targets in the Target Tree, ideas and evaluations in the Idea Graph, representations and assessments in the Cognitive State, and methods in the Cognitive Repertoire. Informed by process accounts of creative thinking [35, 36], we organize operators by their principal function: Framing specifies targets and their requirements; Constructing develops and transforms ideas; Evaluating examines their evidential support and testable consequences; and Learning uses search outcomes to revise the Cognitive State and refine reusable methodological knowledge in the Cognitive Repertoire. These categories allow overlap, and an operator may act on multiple structures. Each operator specifies applicability conditions, reasoning procedure, and expected outputs; control selects applicable operators using the task and Cognitive State. Figure 4 illustrates selected operators and their specialization in chemistry and theoretical physics. Figure 4 Selected Cognitive Operators. Eight representative operators illustrate local reasoning transformations across Framing, Constructing, Evaluating, and Learning. Each card states the operators function and gives examples of its specialization in chemistry and theoretical physics. 2.3.4. Domain Instantiation and Feedback Learning The Cognitive Repertoire combines general heuristics and operators inspired by cognitive science [3] and the science of science [18] with domain-specific research methods. Figure 5 summarizes their development through domain instantiation and feedback learning. Domain instantiation analyzes classic and representative papers to map general reasoning procedures to domain objects, mechanisms, constraints, and validation requirements. This mapping preserves relational structures while grounding their application in disciplinary knowledge and experimental conditions [24, 34]. For example, active hypothesis testing becomes concrete chemistry procedure when two mechanisms predict different sources for product atom: isotope-labeling one reactant and examining the product provides test of their predictions. Entries retain their sources and applicability conditions, distinguishing reported procedures from analytical reconstruction. Feedback learning uses successes, failures, and validation outcomes to refine these entries, drawing inspiration from case-based learning through reuse, testing, revision, and retention [37]. Comparisons across cases and disciplines identify recurring reasoning patterns that inform revisions to general heuristics and operators, following the principle of schema induction from concrete exam7 Figure 5 Domain instantiation and feedback learning. Revised methods can then be instantiated in further domains, with their operating conditions re-examined during transfer, closing the loop. 2.4. Regulating Search through Monitoring and Control Inspired by the monitoringcontrol framework of Nelson and Narens [9] and its extension to reasoning and problem solving [13], Sage-Taiyi uses monitoring to update the Cognitive State from search progress and feedback, and control to decide what to investigate next and how. The resulting decisions guide object-level search and, through the research harness, execution and validation. 2.4.1. Monitoring When targets, ideas, evaluations, or evidence change, monitoring reads the current Cognitive State together with relevant object-level judgments, evaluations, and evidence. It updates the selective representation of scientific understanding and assesses what the changes imply for subsequent search, such as whether current support is sufficient or further work would repeat an unresolved limitation. This provides ongoing verification of evidential support and assumptions, with the assessments recorded in the Cognitive State. Applicable operators from the repertoire support these updates: 𝐶𝑡+1 = Monitor(𝑞, 𝑋𝑡, 𝐶𝑡; R). When no revision is warranted, 𝐶𝑡+1 = 𝐶𝑡. 2.4.2. Grounding Scientific Ideation in Real-World Feedback The research harness translates control decisions into research tasks, invoking ideation when new explanation or design is needed and otherwise proceeding to execution or validation. It refines the selected task into an executable plan with specified inputs, constraints, and evaluation methods, and selects appropriate tools and skills (Figure 6). During ideation, the Target Tree and Idea Graph guide subagents to explore multiple promising reasoning paths in parallel. Returned results are linked to relevant targets, ideas, and conditions in the Evidence State. Monitoring uses this evidence to verify intermediate conclusions and update the Cognitive State, which then guides control over subsequent search. This combination of parallel exploration and ongoing verification aligns with the Agentic Orchestration and Agentic Verification capabilities of Sage-A1.5 [38]. In our research collaborations, this loop connects Sage-Taiyis candidate solutions and search formulations to experiments and simulations, with domain experts participating in idea selection and 9 validation. Tools such as Taiyi-Optimizer support searches within the specified condition or design spaces, while measurements and simulation results inform subsequent research decisions. Detailed experimental results are presented in Section 3. Algorithm 1 summarizes the logical loop; task ends with reviewed ideas or executable plans, or continues to execution and validation, according to its requested output and resource budget. Figure 6 Monitoring and control across research execution. Control uses the Cognitive State and Cognitive Repertoire to guide research tasks, method selection, and branch decisions. The harness invokes ideation when new explanation or design is needed; existing plans can proceed directly to execution or validation. Results enter the Evidence State, while monitoring reads relevant object-level judgments, evaluations, and evidence together with the current Cognitive State to update it. Physical experiments and expert participation follow the corresponding research workflow. 3. Experiments We study Sage-Taiyi through benchmark comparisons and real-world research applications. TaiyiBench assesses its scientific ideation capabilities as an AI co-scientist at different knowledge states, through historical rediscovery and open-ended evaluation of idea quality and diversity (Section 3.1). We also evaluate ideation quality and the use of prior research on AgentIdeaBench and IG-Arena (Section 3.2). We then present five applications in metal catalysis, photochemistry, metamaterials, alloy design, and compressor engineering, showing how Sage-Taiyi helps address practical scientific and engineering problems (Section 3.3). 3.1. Evaluating Scientific Ideation with Taiyi-Bench 3.1.1. Experiment Setup Taiyi-Bench. Taiyi-Bench examines AI co-scientists ability to propose complete, testable research routes given scientists current knowledge. It reconstructs key scientific decisions and their prerequisites from recent published studies* as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), then captures nontrivial decision points central to each studys key innovations, and creates tasks that progressively disclose *We select studies first publicly disclosed on or after 1 March 2026, after GPT-5.6-Sols reported knowledge cutoff (16 February 2026; OpenAI documentation) to reduce training-data contamination risk. 10 established decisions.Nodes are selected to capture nontrivial decision points central to each studys key innovations. Tasks are constructed by progressively disclosing established decisions. At 𝐿0, systems identify the root scientific problem from broad context; subsequent levels specify the problem and disclose preceding decisions. Our evaluation covers 50 papers and 265 caselevel tasks across 10 research domains (i.e., earth science, neuroscience, economics, management, physics, biology, chemistry, environmental science, materials science, and communication engineering). Each task requires 𝐾 self-contained ideas with supporting rationales and discriminating tests. The problem couples composition with solution treatment, quenching, and ageing: promising nominal composition is useful only if practical processing route can realize the desired mechanical properties. Cost also enters candidate selection, making the search joint problem of performance, processing, and material economy. Implementation. Sage-Taiyi proposed four compositionprocessing candidates with different design priorities: strength-priority A, cost/ductility-priority B, lowest-cost C, and experiment-supported baseline (Figure 17a). Experts selected design B, Mg4Y1Nd3Gd0.4Zr, as the starting point for experimentation. Its proposed heat treatment comprised solution treatment at 500 for 14 followed by ageing at 200 for 120 h. Compressor Engineering: Centrifugal Compressor Optimization Problem statement. The compressor-engineering collaboration targets an efficiency improvement for an existing centrifugal compressor design. The relevant choices couple impeller aerodynamics, diffuser matching, and mechanical margins. design that improves one objective can make another constraint more restrictive, so the initial ideation stage explored different tradeoffs before focusing on geometric optimization. Implementation. Sage-Taiyi proposed five routes addressing different aerodynamic and mechanical tradeoffs. The first combined boreless Ti6Al4V backswept splitter impeller with hybrid diffuser, targeting an efficiency greater than 0.76 while retaining aerodynamic and mechanical margins. The second combined high-solidity impeller with 𝑍 = 18 blades, larger vaneless diffuser gap, and boreless architecture to prioritize slip and structural margin. The third combined stronger backsweep and high solidity to reduce impeller-exit absolute Mach number and improve matching to vaned diffuser. This case develops system-level design alternatives into selected compressor geometry, with CFD feedback guiding parameter refinement. Cross-case interpretation. Across the five collaborations, Sage-Taiyi develops scientific ideas and executable search formulations, while the research harness connects them to expert selection, optimization, and experimental or simulation-based evaluation. The resulting feedback guides subsequent research decisions, linking scientific exploration to practical advances in reactions, materials, and engineering designs. 4. Related Work AI Scientists. AI research agents connect literature review, hypothesis generation, and experimentation in workflows that span computational research [54, 47, 55, 56] and laboratory discovery [7, 57, 58, 59, 60]. These systems refine hypotheses or intermediate results through critique [6, 61], carry findings forward through persistent memory and shared representations [46, 62, 63, 64, 65], and use execution results or surrogate models fitted to experimental observations to guide further search [16, 66, 67]. Work focused on scientific ideation integrates evidence from prior research, retrieves and recombines concepts, and checks proposals against existing work [68, 69, 70, 71, 72]. Search methods further develop promising ideas by exploring the literature, tracking evolving idea lineages, or progressively specifying experimental details [73, 74, 75]. Evaluations examine complementary aspects of this process, including the breadth of exploration [76], how experts assess ideas before and after implementation [77, 78], and how new proposals build on prior research [50]. SageTaiyi focuses on how scientific judgments formed along one branch can inform decisions elsewhere in the search. Its revisable Cognitive State retains these judgments together with their supporting ev31 idence and the conditions under which they apply, allowing the agent to revisit them when choosing research targets and methods. Cognitive Science-Inspired Agent Design. Classical research describes problem solving as search over representations and operators [3]; metacognition concerns how this process is monitored and controlled [9, 10]. CoALA organizes memory, internal and external actions, and decision cycles into cognitive architecture for language agents [79]. Generative Agents uses experience retrieval and reflection to support planning [80]. Reflexion retains task feedback as verbal reflections to improve subsequent attempts [81]. Recent work also studies which reasoning methods agents use and how they select them. Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs analyzes reasoning in terms of cognitive elements, including metacognitive controls, knowledge representations, and transformation operations, and finds that models underuse some elements associated with successful reasoning [82]. Chain of Mindset uses meta-agent to select spatial, convergent, divergent, or algorithmic reasoning modes according to the evolving reasoning state [83]. Together with cognitive-science research on creative thinking, metacognition, and scientific reasoning [35, 36, 24, 19, 8, 9, 13, 11, 14, 1, 12, 21], these approaches inform the design of Sage-Taiyis Cognitive Repertoire and state-dependent method selection. Sage-Taiyi maintains methodological heuristics and Cognitive Operators in Cognitive Repertoire and instantiates them for research domains. Monitoring updates the Cognitive State from search outcomes; control uses that state and the repertoire to select targets and methods, revise the Target Tree, and guide idea evolution in the Idea Graph. 5. Conclusion We presented Sage-Taiyi, metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to regulate scientific search. Through monitoring and control, revisable Cognitive State and reusable Cognitive Repertoire guide target selection, idea development, and validation. On Taiyi-Bench, Sage-Taiyi leads all eight metrics, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline. Five expert-guided collaborations further illustrate how its ideas and search formulations connect to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. Future work will refine the Cognitive Repertoire through accumulated research experience and examine its reuse across domains. Building on this repertoire, Sage-Taiyi will scale multi-agent collaboration to explore broader range of high-value solutions within limited time and iteration budgets, aiming to improve the efficiency and quality of scientific discovery.
